studies.title: Low-dose lithium is linked to fewer dementia diagnoses than valproate in older adults
studies.ns_score_reason: a big effect size on a question readers have heard about for years, but observational and the authors are admirably blunt about bias.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Using a "target trial emulation" of multicenter electronic health records in the TriNetX network, researchers compared adults aged 60+ who were taking lithium at genuinely low doses (all serum levels ≤0.40 mmol/L) with matched patients taking valproate, excluding anyone with prior dementia, mild cognitive impairment, bipolar disorder or Parkinson's. After 1:1 propensity matching on 23 covariates (853 per group), all-cause dementia over two years occurred in 3.1% of lithium users versus 8.3% of valproate users (HR 0.38). Mortality was also lower with lithium; hospitalization did not differ.
studies.why_it_matters: Lithium has been floated as a dementia-preventing drug for a decade on thin evidence; this is one of the first analyses to pit low doses against an active comparator rather than against no treatment, which removes some — not all — of the usual confounding. It strengthens the case for the randomized trials now under way rather than settling anything.
studies.pitch_angle: The oldest drug in psychiatry keeps refusing to go away. Open on the strangeness of a 19th-century salt, prescribed at doses so low they would be considered subtherapeutic for mood, showing up again in a dementia analysis — then walk readers through why an "active comparator" design matters and why the authors explicitly refuse to call it causal. Worth calling George Perry (University of Texas at San Antonio), a co-author and long-standing Alzheimer's pathology skeptic, plus an independent pharmacoepidemiologist to pick holes in the depletion-of-susceptibles problem.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a health-policy or pharmacy outlet on target trial emulation itself — how health-record "emulated trials" are being used to triage which old, off-patent drugs are worth the cost of a real RCT, and the growing worry that they generate more hypotheses than anyone can afford to test.
studies.caveats: Observational — cannot establish causation; surveillance and prescribing bias plausible (lithium users get monitored more); modest matched sample (853/group, only 25 dementia events in the lithium arm); diagnoses from clinical coding; 730-day primary follow-up is short for dementia.

studies.title: People with bipolar disorder treated with lithium develop dementia less often than those on valproate
studies.ns_score_reason: a larger, independent cohort pointing the same way as entry 1, which is what lifts it; still observational, and a near-simultaneous use of the same database.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: A retrospective cohort in the TriNetX US records network followed adults aged 45+ with bipolar disorder who started lithium or valproate for the first time between 2000 and 2025; after 1:1 propensity matching, 3056 remained per group. All-cause dementia occurred in 7.1% of lithium users versus 10.8% of valproate users (HR 0.69), with lower risks of unspecified dementia and suicide attempt, and no excess end-stage renal disease or mortality — the two harms clinicians most often cite when avoiding lithium.
studies.why_it_matters: People with bipolar disorder carry elevated dementia risk, and the two first-line mood stabilizers have rarely been compared head-to-head for cognitive outcomes. The kidney-safety null is arguably the more clinically consequential part.
studies.pitch_angle: Two independent teams, two different patient populations, same direction of travel within weeks of each other — lead on the convergence rather than on either paper alone. Open on a 50-something with bipolar disorder weighing a switch off lithium because of kidney fears, then show what the data do and don't say. Call Tsung-Wei Hsu's group (I-Shou University / Kaohsiung Medical University), and pair it with the lithium trialists in the UK for balance.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist psychiatry or medicine outlet: valproate's reputational collapse. Between fetal-exposure restrictions and now cognitive-outcome signals in older adults, is there any population left for whom valproate is the obvious first choice?
studies.caveats: Observational — cannot establish causation; residual confounding by indication (lithium tends to go to more adherent, better-monitored patients); dementia ascertained from ICD coding; no serum-level verification of dose; overlapping data source with entry 1, so the two are not fully independent replications.

studies.title: Depression predicts dementia better than insomnia does — and adding poor sleep tells you almost nothing extra
studies.ns_score_reason: nationally representative, 12 years of follow-up, and it deflates a popular "bad sleep causes dementia" narrative; self-reported symptoms limit it.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Researchers followed 6226 dementia-free older Americans across 13 rounds of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (2011–2023), classifying time-varying symptoms as neither, depression only, insomnia only, or both. Co-occurring symptoms raised dementia hazard versus neither (HR 1.37) and versus insomnia alone (HR 1.25) — but were statistically indistinguishable from depression alone (HR 0.94). Above age 75, the depression-only group actually had a higher hazard than the group with both.
studies.why_it_matters: Insomnia has become the headline risk factor in public conversation about brain health, yet here the sleep component adds essentially nothing once mood is accounted for. For anyone building risk-stratification tools, that suggests asking about mood is the higher-yield question.
studies.pitch_angle: Everyone has read that bad sleep will give them dementia. This cohort says that if you are also low in mood, the sleep part barely moves the needle — and that after 75 the pattern inverts in a way nobody predicted. Open on the familiar 3 a.m. lying-awake scenario and the anxiety it now generates. Call Junxin Li at Johns Hopkins School of Nursing.
studies.wider_angle: A features piece for a general-interest outlet on "risk-factor inflation" in dementia prevention — how a long list of modifiable risks (hearing, sleep, loneliness, air pollution) becomes a moral burden on individuals when much of the variance is shared, correlated and not independently actionable.
studies.caveats: Observational — cannot establish causation; depressive and insomnia symptoms self-reported; incident dementia partly ascertained via proxy report and brief cognitive testing rather than clinical adjudication; reverse causation plausible, as prodromal dementia causes mood and sleep change.

studies.title: Autistic adults report far worse memory and thinking than tests can detect
studies.ns_score_reason: the first synthesis of cognitive aging in autistic adults, with a striking subjective–objective gap; weakened by cross-sectional source studies.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: A systematic review and meta-analysis pooled 15 cross-sectional studies comparing autistic adults (diagnosed or defined by validated trait measures) aged 50+ with neurotypical peers across 13 cognitive constructs. Autistic participants reported substantially greater subjective cognitive difficulty (d = 0.90) — a large effect — while objective performance differed only modestly, and only in processing speed, verbal fluency and working memory (d = −0.28 to −0.38). Most domains showed no difference at all.
studies.why_it_matters: Mid-life and older autistic adults are an almost invisible population in aging research, and the headline finding is reassuring on cognitive decline while raising an awkward clinical question: if autistic people routinely report memory problems that tests do not confirm, how should memory clinics interpret those reports?
studies.pitch_angle: The first generation of adults diagnosed with autism in childhood is now reaching old age, and nobody knows what their brains do next. Lead on the mismatch — people describing serious cognitive struggle that standardized testing shrugs off — and the real possibility that the tests, not the people, are measuring the wrong thing (masking, exhaustion, executive load). Call Lucy Gray and Joshua Stott at UCL.
studies.wider_angle: For a disability or health-services outlet: the coming "autistic aging" gap — care homes, memory clinics and dementia services built around neurotypical norms, and what happens to people who were never diagnosed in the first place.
studies.caveats: Meta-analysis of cross-sectional studies only — no longitudinal data, so nothing can be said about rate of decline; participants over 65 underrepresented; high heterogeneity across analyses; many samples defined by trait questionnaires rather than diagnosis; subjective outcomes self-reported by definition.

studies.title: Loneliness after a stroke is linked to a sharply higher risk of later dementia
studies.ns_score_reason: huge cohort and a clean separation of loneliness from isolation, but UK Biobank's healthy-volunteer skew and self-report limit it.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Among 394,308 UK Biobank participants — 7267 of whom had already had a stroke — researchers tracked mortality, cardiovascular events, dementia and depression over a median 10.2 years. In stroke survivors, feeling lonely was associated with a 67% higher hazard of all-cause dementia (HR 1.67), while objectively being socially isolated was not; isolation instead predicted mortality and cardiovascular death. The excess risks were significantly larger in stroke survivors than in people without stroke, and health behaviors mediated 12–55% of the associations.
studies.why_it_matters: Loneliness and isolation are routinely treated as the same variable; here they split apart, with the subjective feeling — not the objective headcount of contacts — carrying the dementia signal in an already-vulnerable group.
studies.pitch_angle: You can be surrounded by people and still be at risk; you can live alone and not be. Open on a stroke survivor back home with carers in and out of the house all day who still describes herself as lonely, and use the paper to pull apart two things public health keeps conflating. Call Yan-Yan Liang at Guangzhou Medical University's Center for Sleep and Circadian Medicine.
studies.wider_angle: For a health-services or social-policy outlet: post-stroke rehabilitation currently measures walking, speech and swallowing. Should it measure loneliness, and what would an intervention even look like given that befriending trials have a patchy record?
studies.caveats: Observational — cannot establish causation; loneliness and isolation self-reported at a single baseline; 95.4% White and healthier than the general population, so may not generalize; dementia cases from linked hospital and death records; reverse causation possible if early cognitive change drives withdrawal.

studies.title: People with dementia who have sleep problems are at higher risk of suicide — and depression doesn't explain it
studies.ns_score_reason: nationwide data, large N, and a formal mediation analysis that returns a null everyone assumed would be positive; effect size modest.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Linking Taiwan's National Health Insurance database to the national Death Registry, researchers followed 85,920 people aged 50+ newly diagnosed with dementia between 2012 and 2019, of whom 19,982 had documented sleep disturbances, recording 2325 suicide attempts or deaths through 2023. Sleep disturbance was associated with a 12% higher adjusted suicide risk (868 vs 730 per 100,000 person-years). Crucially, mediation analysis found no significant indirect effect through depression — the usual explanation.
studies.why_it_matters: Suicide risk in dementia is underdiscussed and under-screened, and this suggests disturbed sleep is not simply a marker of underlying depression but carries information of its own, pointing at mechanisms such as impulsivity or circadian disruption.
studies.pitch_angle: The assumption has always been that a person with dementia who stops sleeping and then becomes suicidal is depressed. This cohort says the depression link doesn't carry the effect. Frame around what families and clinicians actually ask about at appointments, and the three-visits-to-the-emergency-department signal (aHR 2.54) that is hiding in the same dataset. Call Yu-Pei Lin at An Nan Hospital, China Medical University.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist palliative-care or geriatrics outlet: how rarely suicide risk is assessed after a dementia diagnosis, and how assisted-dying debates intersect with the period just after diagnosis when insight is still intact.
studies.caveats: Observational — cannot establish causation; sleep disturbance inferred from diagnostic codes and prescriptions, so misclassification likely and treated cases may differ systematically from untreated; depression also coded administratively, which weakens the mediation null; single-country health system may not generalize; absolute risk increase is small.

studies.title: Nearly a third of people newly diagnosed with dementia in German family practices get an antipsychotic first
studies.ns_score_reason: nearly 150,000 patients and a genuinely uncomfortable number, though it is a prescribing-pattern study rather than an outcome study.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Using the IQVIA Disease Analyzer database covering 1179 general and 214 specialist practices in Germany (2005–2024), the authors examined what was prescribed in the first year after a first dementia diagnosis in patients aged 65+ with no prior prescriptions. In general practices (n = 94,036), 27.3% received antipsychotics only and just 8.7% received anti-dementia drugs only, with 54.2% receiving neither. In specialist practices (n = 55,341), only 22.2% went untreated and anti-dementia drugs were started first nearly three times as often.
studies.why_it_matters: Antipsychotics carry boxed warnings for increased mortality in older people with dementia, and guidelines place them well down the list. Finding them to be the most common first prescription in primary care is a quantified gap between guideline and practice in a large, well-resourced health system.
studies.pitch_angle: The first drug many people get after a dementia diagnosis is not a dementia drug — it is a sedating antipsychotic with a mortality warning on the label. Open on the family GP appointment where a distressed spouse asks for something to help, and interrogate why where you are diagnosed shapes what you are given. Call Jens Bohlken at the University of Leipzig's ISAP institute.
studies.wider_angle: For a European health-policy outlet: the specialist bottleneck. Germany has one of the densest neurologist networks in Europe and still shows this split — what does it imply for systems where almost all dementia care is primary care?
studies.caveats: Retrospective database study — cannot establish causation or capture clinical reasoning; prescribing may follow severity or behavioral symptoms not recorded in the data; spans two decades over which guidance changed substantially; author discloses consulting fees from Dr. Willmar Schwabe and Lilly, and co-author is employed by IQVIA, which supplies the database.

studies.title: A hidden background signal in the brain's electrical noise predicts who develops Parkinson's or Lewy body dementia
studies.ns_score_reason: a real prognostic signal from a cheap, widely available test, in a well-characterized high-risk cohort; only 26 converters.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Resting EEG was recorded in 134 people with isolated REM sleep behavior disorder — who act out dreams and are at very high risk of later synucleinopathy — and 51 healthy controls; 26 converted to Parkinson's disease or dementia with Lewy bodies during follow-up. By separating rhythmic oscillations from the non-rhythmic "aperiodic" background using FOOOF parameterization, the team showed both posterior 4–8 Hz periodic power (HR 1.34) and aperiodic offset (HR 7.46) independently predicted conversion. Among converters, cognitive scores tracked the aperiodic slope, while motor scores tracked the offset.
studies.why_it_matters: The aperiodic component of EEG was long treated as noise to be discarded. Here it carries the strongest prognostic signal in the dataset — and it comes from a test any sleep lab already runs.
studies.pitch_angle: For decades the flat, fractal background of the EEG was thrown away as junk; it turns out to predict which dream-enacting sleepers go on to develop dementia with Lewy bodies. Open on an RBD clinic, where patients already know they are in a waiting room for neurodegeneration and desperately want to know when. Call Ki-Young Jung at Seoul National University Hospital.
studies.wider_angle: For a neuroscience-literate outlet: the aperiodic revolution. A methods shift (FOOOF and its successors) is quietly rewriting a century of band-power findings across psychiatry, aging and ADHD — how many published "alpha" and "theta" results were actually measuring the background?
studies.caveats: Modest number of converters (26) limits precision of hazard estimates; single-center cohort; follow-up duration not fully specified; cognitive correlations are cross-sectional within converters; needs independent replication before any clinical use.

studies.title: Motor symptoms outrun thinking problems in people destined for Parkinson's — and the gap shows up years early
studies.ns_score_reason: a 766-patient longitudinal cohort with a blind validation set and a personalized progression model; the output is a trial tool rather than a lifestyle finding.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: The FARPRESTO consortium trained a Disease Course Mapping model on cognitive and motor scores from 766 people with isolated REM sleep behavior disorder, extracting three individual parameters — how early, how fast, and whether motor or cognitive decline comes first — then tested it blind in 49 patients who also had dopaminergic imaging and high-density EEG. Motor scores progressed 35% faster than cognitive scores overall; the parameters distinguished converters from non-converters 73% of the time, and those who went on to develop parkinsonism declined earlier than those who developed dementia. Earlier progression correlated with presynaptic dopaminergic loss and with higher theta-band phase synchronization.
studies.why_it_matters: It turns a heterogeneous, decades-long prodrome into three numbers per person, which is exactly what disease-modifying trials need as end points — and it suggests the motor-first/cognition-first split is detectable before either syndrome declares itself.
studies.pitch_angle: Can you tell, years in advance, whether someone will get Parkinson's or dementia? This model says it is partly written into how fast their motor scores drift relative to their cognitive ones. Open with a patient in an RBD clinic doing a routine pegboard test that turns out to carry prognostic weight. Call Dario Arnaldi at the University of Genoa, or Ronald Postuma at McGill for an outside view.
studies.wider_angle: For a drug-development or science-policy outlet: the end-point problem. Why neurodegeneration trials keep failing partly because they measure the wrong thing at the wrong time, and how "disease course mapping" borrowed from Alzheimer's research is spreading across the field.
studies.caveats: Blind test set is small (n = 49) and heavily male; 73% discrimination is useful but not clinically decisive; model trained and tested within largely Italian specialist sleep centers, so may not generalize; biomarker correlations are cross-sectional at baseline.

studies.ns_score_reason: rare combination of cholinergic PET, lesion mapping and mediation analysis in 127 patients; mediation on cross-sectional data is the weak point.

studies.the_study: In 127 people with mid-to-advanced Parkinson's disease but no dementia, researchers combined quantified white-matter lesion burden (FLAIR MRI), basal forebrain volumes and ¹⁸F-FEOBV PET, which maps cholinergic nerve terminals. Lesions around the ventricles — not deep lesions — were associated with reduced cholinergic terminal density in an insular–limbic–frontal–cingulum cluster, and affected key Ch4 projection pathways in 81–88% of patients. Mediation analysis indicated the lesions hit cortical cholinergic terminals directly, plus an indirect route via basal forebrain shrinkage, and that this cholinergic damage statistically carried the link between lesion burden and memory and executive performance.
studies.why_it_matters: It supplies a concrete mechanism linking "small vessel disease" — the incidental white blobs routinely seen on scans of older people — to cognitive decline, and it means blood-pressure and vascular risk management could plausibly protect a neurotransmitter system, not just blood vessels.
studies.pitch_angle: Those white specks your scan report calls "age-related changes" may be cutting cables. Lead on the image: long cholinergic axons running from the base of the brain to the cortex, severed where lesions cluster around the ventricles. Open on a patient told their scan showed "nothing to worry about". Call Nicolaas Bohnen at the University of Michigan.
studies.wider_angle: For a cardiology or general medicine outlet: the brain as a vascular organ. A piece on how midlife hypertension control is being reframed as cognitive medicine, and the awkward fact that white-matter hyperintensities are reported to patients with almost no guidance on what to do about them.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional — mediation analysis cannot establish a causal sequence; single-center; Parkinson's patients without dementia, so findings may not transfer to typical aging or Alzheimer's; basal forebrain volume is an MRI proxy, not a direct cell count.

studies.title: Genetic sleuthing shows many "sporadic" cases of frontotemporal dementia are actually inherited
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean, surprising number from 3524 genomes with direct implications for genetic counseling; the technical framing makes it harder to tell simply.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Researchers ran genome-wide identity-by-descent analysis across 3524 people of European ancestry on the ALS–frontotemporal dementia spectrum, from Australia, New Zealand and the UK. They found 793 pairs of first- to sixth-degree relatives, 31.5% of them previously unrecognized; 15.9% of people classified as having "sporadic" FTD and 5.5% of sporadic ALS turned out to be genetically related to another affected person in the cohort. Reconstructing 73 new pedigrees from apparently unrelated patients also revealed cross-continent founder networks for SOD1 and C9orf72, and narrowed a candidate locus on chromosome 13q21.33.
studies.why_it_matters: "Sporadic" has always been a diagnosis of ignorance — it means no known affected relatives, not no inheritance. Quantifying how often hidden relatedness lurks behind that label changes how families should be counseled and makes previously underpowered pedigrees usable for gene discovery.
studies.pitch_angle: Two patients in different countries, told their disease was random bad luck, turn out to be second cousins. Open on exactly that and use it to explain reduced penetrance — why a family can carry a dementia gene for generations without anyone noticing. Call Kelly Williams or Ian Blair at Macquarie University Brain Institute.
studies.wider_angle: For a genetics or bioethics outlet: consumer DNA databases and research cohorts are now capable of telling people things about inherited neurodegenerative risk that nobody consented to learn, including about relatives they have never met. Who gets told what?
studies.caveats: European-ancestry cohort only — findings may not generalize to other populations; relatedness within a recruited research cohort may overstate rates in the wider patient population; the new 13q21.33 candidate locus is based on a single extended pedigree and remains unconfirmed; clinical classification of "sporadic" varies between contributing centers.

studies.title: Sleeping light instead of deep is linked to early damage in the brain's small blood vessels
studies.ns_score_reason: home sleep monitoring plus sensitive diffusion imaging in a population cohort is a neat combination, but cross-sectional and N = 154.
studies.the_study: In 154 participants of the population-based Hamburg City Health Study (mean age 63, 42% women), researchers combined portable WatchPAT home sleep diagnostics with brain MRI measures sensitive to very early microstructural change. A sleep profile weighted toward light sleep relative to deep sleep was associated with higher peak-width of skeletonized mean diffusivity — an early marker of small vessel disease — and with thinner cortex. REM sleep proportion showed no such association, and neither did the conventional markers of white matter hyperintensities or perivascular space volume.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the brain consequences of shallow sleep may be visible before anything shows up on a standard clinical scan — useful for designing prevention trials, though it cannot say whether poor sleep damages vessels or damaged vessels fragment sleep.
studies.pitch_angle: The damage may be happening before the scan can see it. Lead on PSMD, the diffusion measure that picks up microvascular change while the conventional read-out still says "normal", and on the fact that deep sleep — not REM, the glamorous stage — carried the signal. Open on someone in their sixties wearing a finger-worn sleep monitor at home for a week. Call Bastian Cheng at University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf.
studies.wider_angle: For a consumer-tech or health outlet: your smartwatch reports "deep sleep" every morning. A piece on what these devices actually measure versus polysomnography, and whether research-grade home monitors like WatchPAT are about to make population sleep–brain studies routine.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional — cannot establish causation, and reverse causality is explicitly acknowledged by the authors; small N (154); single city cohort; sleep staging derived from a peripheral-arterial-tone device rather than full polysomnography; multiple imaging outcomes tested with several nulls.

studies.the_study: The multicenter Brain Aging and Cognition in Epilepsy (BrACE) study assessed instrumental activities of daily living with the Functional Activities Questionnaire in 57 people with epilepsy aged 55+ (mean 66.6). Some 38.6% had impairment at the level used to define mild cognitive impairment and 17.5% at dementia level. Temporal lobe localization, epilepsy onset before age 60 and lower education independently predicted impairment; difficulties clustered in financial and memory-dependent tasks. In the 13 followed for two years, four worsened significantly.
studies.why_it_matters: Epilepsy in later life is usually managed around seizure counts; this suggests a substantial minority are quietly losing the ability to manage money and medication, which is the practical face of cognitive decline.
studies.pitch_angle: The seizures are controlled, the clinic appointment lasts ten minutes, and nobody asks whether the patient can still do their own banking. Open on the finding that financial tasks fail first, and on the counterintuitive detail that earlier-onset epilepsy — decades of it — predicted worse function in old age. Call Ifrah Zawar at the University of Virginia or Carrie McDonald at UC San Diego.
studies.wider_angle: For a geriatrics or aging-policy outlet: financial capacity as the canary for cognitive decline across many conditions, and why banks, not neurologists, often spot it first.
studies.caveats: Small N (57) and very small longitudinal subsample (13); cross-sectional for the main analyses; functional impairment rated by questionnaire, often by informants; multicenter but specialist epilepsy centers, so likely enriched for complex cases; wide confidence intervals on the odds ratios.

studies.the_study: Researchers at the Danish Dementia Research Centre assessed 143 adults aged 55+ (60 community-dwelling, 83 audiology clinic patients) with pure-tone audiometry, two subjective cognitive complaint scales, a depression scale and tests of episodic memory and processing speed. People with moderate-to-severe hearing loss reported more cognitive complaints and performed worse on memory and processing speed. But once age, sex, depressive symptoms and objective test scores were entered into regression models, hearing level no longer had an independent effect on subjective complaints.
studies.why_it_matters: Hearing loss is currently the single largest modifiable risk factor in the Lancet Commission's dementia list, and "I can't remember" complaints from people who are hard of hearing are a common clinic presentation. This suggests the complaint is substantially carried by mood and genuine cognitive performance rather than by deafness itself.
studies.pitch_angle: If you cannot hear what was said, you cannot remember it — and you may conclude your memory is going. Open in an audiology waiting room with a patient convinced they are developing dementia, then unpack what disappears when depression is accounted for. Call Asmus Vogel at Rigshospitalet's Danish Dementia Research Centre.
studies.wider_angle: For a health or consumer outlet: the hearing-aid-and-dementia question after ACHIEVE. Do the devices protect cognition, who benefits, and how much of the public messaging has outrun the evidence?
studies.caveats: Small N (143) and mixed recruitment from two very different sources; cross-sectional — cannot establish causation; primary outcomes self-reported; pure-tone audiometry measures tone detection, not speech-in-noise ability, which may be the more cognitively relevant measure; correlations are weak (rho ≈ 0.21–0.25).

studies.the_study: Researchers measured mitochondrial respiration in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 166 spouses caring for a partner with dementia, alongside attachment style, and tracked depressive symptoms seven months later, adjusting for baseline depression and health covariates. Spare respiratory capacity — the cells' reserve energy capability — predicted future depressive symptoms, but only in caregivers scoring at or above average on attachment anxiety (interaction b = −1.11, p = .016).
studies.why_it_matters: It is an early, testable attempt to link how a person relates to their partner with how their cells generate energy under chronic stress; at this stage it opens a line of enquiry rather than changing anything.
studies.pitch_angle: Your relationship style may determine whether your cells' energy reserves show up in your mood. Open on a spouse caring at home for a partner who no longer recognizes them — the most studied chronic stressor in psychology — and on why mitochondria have become the fashionable candidate for translating stress into depression. Call Christopher Fagundes at Rice University.
studies.wider_angle: For a psychology or long-read outlet: "mitochondrial psychiatry" — the rapid rise of cellular bioenergetics as an explanation for depression, and whether the field is repeating the pattern of earlier biomarker booms that failed to replicate.
studies.caveats: Observational — cannot establish causation; N = 166 with the key result resting on a single moderation effect, which is the sort of finding that replicates poorly; mitochondrial measures taken once at baseline only; depressive symptoms self-reported; short follow-up (7 months); caregiver samples skew toward older, white, volunteering spouses.

studies.the_study: Fourteen African Caribbean people in the UK with experience of supporting a family member with memory loss were interviewed about barriers to seeking help, analyzed with reflexive thematic analysis. Participants described a historically rooted self-reliance and stoicism, attribution of memory loss to ordinary aging or personal quirks, stigma around mental difficulty, an expectation that daughters would provide care, and explicit fear that racism would produce worse or culturally insensitive treatment. The authors argue funding should flow to African Caribbean community organizations to lead change, given mistrust of mainstream institutions.
studies.why_it_matters: This group has a higher incidence of dementia than White Britons yet lower service use; most previous research lumped ethnic minority groups together, obscuring the specific history that drives the gap.
studies.pitch_angle: Higher risk, later diagnosis — and a reluctance to seek help that participants trace directly to how the NHS and wider society treated their generation on arrival. Open on a daughter masking her mother's symptoms from services. Call Gerard Riley at the University of Birmingham's School of Psychology.
studies.wider_angle: For a news or social-affairs outlet: as the Windrush generation reaches the ages of peak dementia risk, Britain faces a wave of late-presenting cases in a community that does not trust the services designed to help. studies.caveats: Small qualitative sample (N = 14) — not designed to be representative; self-reported perceptions; recruited in one region of the UK; no comparison group; findings describe barriers rather than testing any intervention.

studies.the_study: A retrospective analysis of electronic records from 284 people with advanced dementia enrolled in a home-based palliative care service in Singapore examined "final place of care" — where care happened in the last three days of life — rather than the usual metric of place of death. Home accounted for 81.7%, with 9.2% each in hospital and inpatient hospice. Counterintuitively, *better* biological and functional status predicted hospital admission, while discomfort, oral feeding difficulties, psychosocial problems and family unemployment predicted late, unplanned hospice transfers. Stable sociodemographic factors, which predict place of death, had no effect on final place of care.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests end-of-life trajectories in dementia are driven by acute, fluctuating circumstances rather than the fixed patient characteristics that policy tends to use for planning.
studies.pitch_angle: The people who get moved to hospital in their final days are the ones who look healthiest — because dementia's dying trajectory is so unpredictable that nobody recognizes the end has arrived. Open on a family calling an ambulance at 2 a.m. after months of coping. Call Ri Yin Tay at Dover Park Hospice and Lancaster University.
studies.wider_angle: For a health-policy or long-form outlet: place of death is the quality metric every health system reports. This study argues it is close to meaningless for dementia — a piece on how choosing the wrong indicator distorts an entire service.
studies.caveats: Retrospective record review of a single specialist home palliative care service — cannot establish causation and may not generalize to other systems or to people without such a service; 284 participants; stated preferences recorded in notes, with unknown reliability; Singapore's family-care norms and housing differ sharply from many Western settings.

studies.the_study: Australian researchers interviewed people with Down syndrome and their families about their understanding of dementia and their experience of diagnostic pathways, using applied thematic analysis with inductive and deductive coding. People with Down syndrome understood the concept of dementia. Families knew about the strong link between Down syndrome and Alzheimer's — roughly a lifetime certainty of Alzheimer's pathology, given trisomy of the amyloid precursor protein gene — but several were reluctant to raise it with their relative, and most lacked confidence in existing diagnostic pathways.
studies.why_it_matters: This is the population with the highest genetic risk of Alzheimer's in the world, now living into their sixties, and the finding undercuts a common clinical assumption that people with intellectual disability cannot engage with their own diagnosis.
studies.pitch_angle: The people most protected from the conversation turn out to be the ones who understand it. Open on an adult with Down syndrome who knows exactly what dementia is, and a family who have decided not to mention it. Tie to the fact that Down syndrome cohorts are now central to Alzheimer's prevention trials. Call Amy Brodtmann at Monash University.
studies.wider_angle: For a disability or medical-ethics outlet: the right to know your own diagnosis. How "therapeutic non-disclosure" persists in intellectual disability care decades after it was abandoned in cancer medicine.
studies.caveats: Small qualitative study — sample size not stated in the abstract; single health service in Melbourne; self-reported perceptions; no quantitative outcomes; families who volunteer for dementia research are likely more informed than average, so may not generalize.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- **Mood keeps absorbing the variance assigned to other risk factors.** "Depression predicts dementia better than insomnia does" (PMID 42144138) and "Hearing loss makes people feel their memory is failing — but tests suggest something else is going on" (PMID 42126868) both show a headline exposure losing its independent effect once depressive symptoms are in the model. That extends last month's within-person finding that a bad mood week knocks about a point off an MCI patient's cognitive score (PMID 40859820): depression is not just a comorbidity in this literature, it is a persistent confounder of how other risks are estimated.
- **Iatrogenic harm remains a live seam.** "Nearly a third of people newly diagnosed with dementia in German family practices get an antipsychotic first" (PMID 42772309) sits directly alongside the previous digest's "Most cases of hypersexuality in neurological illness are caused by the treatment" (PMID 42330690) — two different routes to the same uncomfortable point, that a sizeable share of the behavioral burden in dementia and Parkinson's is prescription-shaped.
- **Caregiver biology, continued.** "A biological marker in caregivers' blood predicts depression months later" (PMID 42804652) keeps the relational-physiology thread running from last month's heart rate synchrony study (PMID 42398884) and the caregiver-mortality reappraisal (PMID 42721295), all three in the same small cluster of journals.

**Advances**
- **Lithium moves from advocacy to data.** Last month's "The case for reviving lithium — at a fraction of the psychiatric dose" (PMID 42268602) was a narrative review arguing for a trial that has not run. This month two active-comparator emulated trials in the same EHR network report in the same direction: low-dose lithium versus valproate in over-60s (PMID 42372694, HR 0.38) and lithium versus valproate in bipolar disorder (PMID 42349060, HR 0.69), the latter also returning a kidney-safety null. The "mechanism-rich, trial-poor" pattern logged in topic memory has not broken — but the observational evidence is now comparator-controlled rather than versus no treatment.
- **TriNetX as the field's default instrument.** The COMISA study (PMID 42640940) used it last month; both lithium papers use it this month. Worth flagging as a methods story in its own right, since entries 1 and 2 are not independent replications.
- **Epilepsy and cognitive aging moves from pathology to function.** Previous entries addressed hemisphere-asymmetric tau in historical brains (PMID 42715912) and the dissolution of the epilepsy–depression association under competing-risk adjustment (PMID 42155275). "Four in ten older people with epilepsy struggle with everyday tasks" (PMID 42704320) now puts an everyday-function number on the same population.
- **Neurodivergent aging broadens beyond intellectual disability.** The previous batch established burden and measurement failure in intellectual disability (PMIDs 42623159, 42609160, 42659675). This batch adds the first synthesis of cognitive aging in autistic adults (PMID 42815817) and the diagnostic-communication problem in Down syndrome (PMID 42725843) — same structural gap, two new populations, and in both cases the issue is whether the instruments and the conversations are fit for purpose.
- **Small vessel disease gains a neurotransmitter mechanism.** "Tiny white-matter lesions damage the brain's acetylcholine supply lines" (PMID 42117428) and "Sleeping light instead of deep is linked to early damage in the brain's small blood vessels" (PMID 42779207) advance the vascular-to-cognition chain sketched last month in the CADASIL mouse and postmortem work (PMID 41622715), this time in living humans with imaging rather than in a rare genetic model.

**Counterpoints**
- **Insomnia's standing as a dementia risk factor takes a knock.** "Depression predicts dementia better than insomnia does — and adding poor sleep tells you almost nothing extra" (PMID 42144138) cuts against the framing of last month's COMISA study, where apnea-plus-insomnia carried a 34% excess dementia hazard (PMID 42640940). Both flag reverse causation; neither resolves it, but the NHATS result suggests the insomnia component may be doing less work than the sleep-medicine literature implies.
- **Depression as universal explanation fails a formal test.** "People with dementia who have sleep problems are at higher risk of suicide — and depression doesn't explain it" (PMID 42790647) returns a mediation null where the previous digest's mood-cognition work (PMID 40859820) would predict depression to be the connecting variable.

**New themes**
- The isolated REM sleep behavior disorder prodrome as a prediction testbed: aperiodic EEG signal (PMID 42747400) and personalized disease course mapping (PMID 42213896) — nothing comparable in the previous batch.
- Hidden heritability behind "sporadic" diagnosis: identity-by-descent analysis in FTD/ALS (PMID 42789481).
- End-of-life and access inequity as measurable service questions: African Caribbean help-seeking (PMID 40939289) and final place of care in Singapore (PMID 40913758).
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Several studies in this batch each take a named "modifiable risk factor" for dementia and find that what matters is the subjective state rather than the objective exposure — or that the risk shrinks once mood is in the model. Insomnia adds essentially nothing to dementia prediction once depression is accounted for (PMID 42144138); after a stroke, feeling lonely predicts dementia while being socially isolated does not (PMID 42119905); hearing level loses its independent link to cognitive complaints once depressive symptoms and actual test scores are included (PMID 42126868). Running the other way, "Autistic adults report far worse memory and thinking than tests can detect" (PMID 42815817) shows the mismatch in reverse, with a large subjective deficit and only modest objective one.

**Why pitch this now:** The public prevention message is built on a checklist of discrete, independently actionable risks — hearing, sleep, social contact — and four studies published within weeks suggest those items are heavily correlated, partly interchangeable with mood, and not separable in the way the checklist implies.

**Angle:** A reported feature on what the dementia risk-factor list is actually measuring, following one or two of these risks from epidemiological estimate to the clinic room to the health-promotion poster, and asking researchers what survives when you adjust for how people feel. For a general readership that has been told to buy hearing aids, fix their sleep and see more friends, and is quietly keeping score.

**Potential headlines:**
- Three dementia risk factors that shrink when you measure them more carefully
- Loneliness counts, having people around doesn't — and sleep barely registers next to mood
- The dementia prevention checklist is asking you to fix things it can't tell apart

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — Mind is already running the individual studies; a features slot can carry the cross-study reordering and the measurement argument that no single item supports.
- **The Guardian science desk** — the Lancet Commission framing is British, widely promoted in UK public health messaging, and the feature is in effect an evidence audit of it.
- **The Atlantic** — strong fit for the moral-burden strand: health advice that converts shared, correlated risk into personal responsibility.
- **Undark** — would take seriously the methods spine here, that adjusting for depression repeatedly dissolves effects the field has been promoting as independent.

# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Dementia — October 2026
**Checked:** 2026-10-06 | **Studies reviewed:** 18
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind dementia digest (run 2026-10-06)

---

### Study 1: Low-dose lithium is linked to fewer dementia diagnoses than valproate in older adults
**PMID:** 42372694 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

All study facts check out: TriNetX target trial emulation, age ≥60, serum lithium ≤0.40 mmol/L, 23 covariates, 853 per matched cohort, 3.1% vs 8.3%, HR 0.38, lower mortality, null for hospitalization, 730-day primary outcome. Framing is appropriately non-causal and mirrors the authors' own hedging.

**Issue A. NS fit score sits above what the evidence base supports** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — a big effect size on a question readers have heard about for years, but observational and the authors are admirably blunt about bias."
- **Abstract says:** "All-cause dementia occurred in 25/795 (3.1%) lithium versus 69/832 (8.3%) valproate users"; "These observational findings cannot distinguish a direct effect from prescribing or surveillance bias, depletion of susceptibles, or differential healthcare engagement; they are hypothesis-generating"
- **Problem:** The entire headline result rests on 94 dementia events (25 of them in the lithium arm) in an uncontrolled retrospective EHR cohort whose authors explicitly label it hypothesis-generating. A 7 implies a stronger evidence base than that; the digest's own caveat line concedes the point.
- **Suggested fix:** "**NS fit:** 6/10 — a big effect size on a question readers have heard about for years, but observational, built on only 94 dementia events, and the authors are admirably blunt about bias."

*Note:* "a long-standing Alzheimer's pathology skeptic" (describing co-author George Perry) is unverifiable from abstract only — it is a characterization of a person, not a study claim, so it is not scored as an issue, but check it before the pitch goes out.

---

### Study 2: People with bipolar disorder treated with lithium develop dementia less often than those on valproate
**PMID:** 42349060 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Numbers are accurate: 3056 per matched group, 7.1% vs 10.8%, HR 0.689, lower unspecified dementia and suicide attempt, nulls for vascular dementia, mortality and ESRD.

**Issue A. "Novelty" label not supported by the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Overturns prior research"
- **Abstract says:** "few studies have directly compared subsequent dementia risk between BD patients treated with lithium and valproate, the two first-line mood stabilizers."
- **Problem:** The authors position this as filling an evidence gap, not as contradicting an established finding. Nothing in the abstract identifies prior research being overturned.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** First direct head-to-head comparison"

**Issue B. Wider angle edges into a prescribing recommendation from observational data** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Between fetal-exposure restrictions and now cognitive-outcome signals in older adults, is there any population left for whom valproate is the obvious first choice?"
- **Abstract says:** "though observational data preclude causality inferences."
- **Problem:** Framed as a question, but it invites a first-line prescribing conclusion from a propensity-matched claims analysis with acknowledged confounding by indication. Note also that the authors themselves overreach here ("These findings support lithium as a preferred long-term mood stabilizer"), which is worth flagging to the writer rather than inheriting.
- **Suggested fix:** "...a piece on how much weight prescribers should put on observational cognitive-outcome signals when the authors themselves concede causality cannot be inferred."

---

### Study 3: Depression predicts dementia better than insomnia does — and adding poor sleep tells you almost nothing extra
**PMID:** 42144138 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 6226, 13 rounds of NHATS (2011–2023), HRs 1.37 / 1.25 / 0.94 and the age-75 reversal are all reported correctly.

**Issue A. Framing drops half of the authors' own conclusion** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Insomnia has become the headline risk factor in public conversation about brain health, yet here the sleep component adds essentially nothing once mood is accounted for."
- **Abstract says:** "Findings support joint assessment of mood and sleep symptoms to identify older adults at elevated dementia risk and suggest that depressive symptoms may be more informative than insomnia symptoms for risk stratification in later life, with heterogeneity by age."
- **Problem:** The digest reports only the second half of the conclusion and builds the headline and "Why it matters" around deflating sleep. The authors explicitly endorse *joint* assessment; the co-occurring group still carried a higher hazard than neither-symptom (HR 1.37) and than insomnia-only (HR 1.25). An editor reading this would think the paper says sleep is irrelevant, which it does not.
- **Suggested fix:** "Insomnia has become the headline risk factor in public conversation about brain health, yet here co-occurring symptoms were statistically indistinguishable from depression alone — the authors still recommend assessing mood and sleep together, but conclude depressive symptoms are the more informative of the two for risk stratification."

**Issue B. NS fit score with wholly self-reported exposures** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — nationally representative, 12 years of follow-up, and it deflates a popular 'bad sleep causes dementia' narrative; self-reported symptoms limit it."
- **Abstract says:** "Depressive symptoms and insomnia symptoms were self-reported"; "Incident dementia was determined using self/proxy reports, cognitive testing, and the AD8."
- **Problem:** Both exposure and (partly) outcome are self- or proxy-reported, and the "deflation" framing is the part of the conclusion the authors did not actually draw (see Issue A). A 7 is one point generous.
- **Suggested fix:** "**NS fit:** 6/10 — nationally representative with 12 years of follow-up, but exposures are self-reported and dementia is partly proxy-ascertained."

---

### Study 4: Autistic adults report far worse memory and thinking than tests can detect
**PMID:** 42815817 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

The 15 cross-sectional studies, 13 constructs, d = 0.90 subjective effect, and d = −0.28 to −0.38 for processing speed, verbal fluency and working memory are all reproduced correctly, as is the "first synthesis" claim and the under-65 and heterogeneity limitations.

**Issue A. NS fit score rests on a self-report effect in cross-sectional source studies** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — the first synthesis of cognitive aging in autistic adults, with a striking subjective–objective gap; weakened by cross-sectional source studies."
- **Abstract says:** "Fifteen cross-sectional studies were included"; "interpretation is limited by underrepresentation of participants over 65, and the absence of longitudinal studies"; "Heterogeneity was high across several analyses."
- **Problem:** The headline number (d = 0.90) is pooled self-report from cross-sectional studies, many of which used trait questionnaires rather than diagnosis, with high heterogeneity and no longitudinal data. The digest's caveats are honest, but the score doesn't reflect them.
- **Suggested fix:** "**NS fit:** 6/10 — the first synthesis of cognitive ageing in autistic adults, with a striking subjective–objective gap; the headline effect is pooled self-report from cross-sectional studies with high heterogeneity."

---

### Study 5: Loneliness after a stroke is linked to a sharply higher risk of later dementia
**PMID:** 42119905 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 394,308, 7267 with prevalent stroke, median 10.2 years, loneliness–dementia HR 1.67, 95.4% White: all correct.

**Issue A. Interaction significance overstated, and applied to the wrong outcome** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "The excess risks were significantly larger in stroke survivors than in people without stroke, and health behaviors mediated 12–55% of the associations."
- **Abstract says:** "These associations—particularly for all-cause mortality (Pinteraction = 0.006) and CVD mortality (Pinteraction = 0.042)—were more pronounced in stroke survivors than in those without stroke."
- **Problem:** Only two interaction p-values are reported, both for mortality outcomes. The abstract gives no evidence that the *dementia* association — the subject of the headline and the whole pitch — was significantly amplified by stroke. As written, a reader assumes the stroke-specific dementia amplification was demonstrated.
- **Suggested fix:** "The stroke-versus-no-stroke difference reached statistical significance for all-cause mortality and cardiovascular mortality; no interaction test is reported for dementia."

**Issue B. Mediation percentages merged across two different exposures** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "health behaviors mediated 12–55% of the associations"
- **Abstract says:** "Health behaviours mediated a substantial proportion of the associations for social isolation (32-55%) and loneliness (12-50%) with most outcomes."
- **Problem:** The digest fuses two separate ranges into one, producing a figure (12–55%) that appears in the abstract for neither exposure.
- **Suggested fix:** "health behaviours mediated 32–55% of the social-isolation associations and 12–50% of the loneliness associations"

**Issue C. Isolation's association with depression dropped** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "isolation instead predicted mortality and cardiovascular death"
- **Abstract says:** "social isolation was independently associated with higher risks of all-cause mortality (HR: 1.41), CVD mortality (HR: 1.57), and depression (HR: 1.35)."
- **Problem:** Omitting depression sharpens the "isolation is about the body, loneliness is about the brain" contrast the pitch leans on. Both exposures were associated with depression.
- **Suggested fix:** "isolation instead predicted mortality, cardiovascular death and depression"

---

### Study 6: People with dementia who have sleep problems are at higher risk of suicide — and depression doesn't explain it
**PMID:** 42790647 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

85,920 / 19,982 / 2325 events, aHR 1.12, 868.3 vs 729.7 per 100,000 person-years, and the non-significant indirect effect through depression are all accurate.

**Issue A. Emergency department figure loses its denominator** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the three-visits-to-the-emergency-department signal (aHR 2.54) that is hiding in the same dataset"
- **Abstract says:** "frequent emergency department visits were additional predictors (≥3 visits/year: aHR, 2.54; 95% CI, 2.20-2.94)"
- **Problem:** The threshold is three or more visits *per year*, not three visits in total. A reporter writing from the digest alone would get this wrong.
- **Suggested fix:** "the three-or-more-emergency-department-visits-a-year signal (aHR 2.54)"

**Issue B. Named mechanisms are the digest's, not the paper's** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "pointing at mechanisms such as impulsivity or circadian disruption"
- **Abstract says:** "This association persisted after accounting for depression, suggesting involvement of other mechanisms."
- **Problem:** The abstract names no candidate mechanism. Presenting impulsivity and circadian disruption without attribution reads as a study finding. (Relatedly, the "New mechanism" novelty tag is generous for what is a null mediation result.)
- **Suggested fix:** "pointing at mechanisms the authors leave unspecified — a writer could put impulsivity and circadian disruption to them as candidates."

---

### Study 7: Nearly a third of people newly diagnosed with dementia in German family practices get an antipsychotic first
**PMID:** 42772309 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Practice counts, date range, cohort sizes (94,036 / 55,341), 54.2% / 27.3% / 8.7% / 22.2% and the 16.0% vs 5.6% ratio ("nearly three times") all check out. Industry funding and author disclosures are correctly carried into Caveats.

**Issue A. "Nearly a third" rounds up, and conflates "only" with "first"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Nearly a third of people newly diagnosed with dementia in German family practices get an antipsychotic first"
- **Abstract says:** "In general practices, 54.2% received neither drug class, 27.3% antipsychotics only, 8.7% anti-dementia drugs only."
- **Problem:** Two small slips in one headline. 27.3% is "more than a quarter", not "nearly a third"; and the abstract's 27.3% figure is patients who received antipsychotics *exclusively*, which is not the same category as patients who received an antipsychotic *first*. The abstract reports sequence only as "anti-dementia treatment was initiated first more often (16.0% vs. 5.6%)."
- **Suggested fix:** "More than a quarter of people newly diagnosed with dementia in German family practices get an antipsychotic and nothing else"

---

### Study 8: A hidden background signal in the brain's electrical noise predicts who develops Parkinson's or Lewy body dementia
**PMID:** 42747400 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

134 iRBD / 51 controls, 26 converters, FOOOF parameterization, HR 1.342 and HR 7.457, and the MoCA-K/slope and MDS-UPDRS-III/offset correlations among converters are all accurate.

**Issue A. "Independently" is not stated in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "both posterior 4–8 Hz periodic power (HR 1.34) and aperiodic offset (HR 7.46) independently predicted conversion"
- **Abstract says:** "Survival analyses showed that higher posterior periodic 4-8 Hz power (hazard ratio = 1.342...) and offset (hazard ratio = 7.457...) were associated with phenoconversion risk."
- **Problem:** Whether the two measures were entered in the same model and remained significant after mutual adjustment is not stated. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "both posterior 4–8 Hz periodic power (HR 1.34) and aperiodic offset (HR 7.46) were associated with conversion risk"

**Issue B. "Strongest prognostic signal" compares hazard ratios on different scales** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Here it carries the strongest prognostic signal in the dataset"
- **Abstract says:** HRs of 1.342 (periodic 4–8 Hz power) and 7.457 (offset), with no statement ranking them.
- **Problem:** Hazard ratios for two differently scaled continuous predictors are not directly comparable; a larger HR can simply reflect a smaller measurement unit. The abstract makes no "strongest" claim.
- **Suggested fix:** "Here it carries a large and statistically robust prognostic signal — the authors note it adds information beyond conventional band power"

**Issue C. "Single-centre" descriptor not supported** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "single-center cohort"
- **Abstract says:** Author affiliations span Seoul National University Hospital, Kyung Hee University Hospital at Gangdong and Kangbuk Samsung Hospital; recruitment sites are not described.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only, and the affiliation list suggests more than one recruiting centre may be involved.
- **Suggested fix:** "recruitment sites not specified in the abstract; check whether this is single- or multi-centre"

---

### Study 9: Motor symptoms outrun thinking problems in people destined for Parkinson's — and the gap shows up years early
**PMID:** 42213896 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues (two Moderate — revise before pitching)

The study description is otherwise solid: 766 training patients, three parameters (τ, α, ω), blind set of 49 with DAT imaging and HD-EEG, 35% faster motor progression, 73% discrimination, parkinsonism converters worsening earlier than dementia converters, and the dopaminergic and theta-synchronization correlations.

**Issue A. Headline overstates both the population and the timing** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Motor symptoms outrun thinking problems in people destined for Parkinson's — and the gap shows up years early"
- **Abstract says:** "Motor scores progress 35% faster than cognitive scores in our iRBD cohort"; "Converter iRBD patients exhibited a faster and earlier disease progression than non-converters."
- **Problem:** Two problems. The 35% figure is for the whole iRBD cohort, most of whom did not convert — not for "people destined for Parkinson's". And no lead time in years is given anywhere in the abstract, so "the gap shows up years early" is unsupported.
- **Suggested fix:** "Motor symptoms outrun thinking problems in people with the sleep disorder that precedes Parkinson's"

**Issue B. Pitch attributes the PD-versus-dementia split to the wrong model parameter** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Can you tell, years in advance, whether someone will get Parkinson's or dementia? This model says it is partly written into how fast their motor scores drift relative to their cognitive ones."
- **Abstract says:** "Patients with iRBD who developed parkinsonism worsened earlier than those who developed dementia."
- **Problem:** The abstract distinguishes the two converter groups by *time-shift* (how early they started to decline), not by the motor-versus-cognitive spacing parameter. The pitch hook names a result the study did not report. The abstract also notes converters showed earlier motor than cognitive worsening "regardless of the clinical diagnosis of overt parkinsonism" — i.e. explicitly not a PD-versus-dementia discriminator.
- **Suggested fix:** "Can you tell in advance how fast someone with iRBD will decline? This model says those who go on to parkinsonism start declining earlier than those who go on to dementia — and does it with three numbers per patient."

---

### Study 10: Tiny white-matter lesions damage the brain's acetylcholine supply lines — and that's what drags cognition down in Parkinson's
**PMID:** 42117428 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues (one Moderate)

N = 127, mid-to-advanced PD without dementia, FLAIR/UBO lesion quantification, basal forebrain volumetry, ¹⁸F-FEOBV PET, the insular–limbic–frontal–cingulum cluster, 81–88% Ch4 pathway involvement, the direct and basal-forebrain-mediated routes, and stronger mediation for memory and executive function are all reported accurately.

**Issue A. Headline asserts causation from cross-sectional mediation** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Tiny white-matter lesions damage the brain's acetylcholine supply lines — and that's what drags cognition down in Parkinson's"
- **Abstract says:** "Mediation analyses indicated that periventricular lesions had a direct effect on cortical terminal integrity... Our findings indicate that periventricular white matter lesions contribute to cognitive vulnerability"; the design is a single-timepoint imaging study, as the digest's own caveat concedes ("Cross-sectional — mediation analysis cannot establish a causal sequence").
- **Problem:** "Damage" and "that's what drags cognition down" are causal verbs applied to statistical mediation on cross-sectional data, directly contradicting the digest's own Caveats line. "Tiny" is also the digest's addition — lesion size is not characterized in the abstract, only burden.
- **Suggested fix:** "White-matter lesions track with damage to the brain's acetylcholine supply lines — and that may be what links them to cognition in Parkinson's"

**Issue B. Prevention leap in "Why it matters"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "it means blood-pressure and vascular risk management could plausibly protect a neurotransmitter system, not just blood vessels"
- **Abstract says:** "White matter lesion burden may represent a mechanistically meaningful biomarker for predicting cognitive trajectories and informing targeted interventions in Parkinson's disease."
- **Problem:** The study tested no intervention and no vascular risk factor. "Could plausibly" is hedged, but it is the digest's extrapolation, not the paper's.
- **Suggested fix:** "the authors suggest lesion burden could become a biomarker for predicting cognitive trajectories — whether modifying vascular risk changes anything is untested here"

---

### Study 11: Genetic sleuthing shows many "sporadic" cases of frontotemporal dementia are actually inherited
**PMID:** 42789481 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

3524 individuals, European ancestry, 793 relative pairs, 31.5% previously unrecognized, 15.9% sporadic FTD and 5.5% sporadic ALS, 73 new IBD-defined pedigrees, SOD1 and C9orf72 founder networks, and the 13q21.33 locus in a single five-person pedigree are all correct — including the digest's careful caveat that the locus is unconfirmed.

**Issue A. "Many" overstates one in six** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Genetic sleuthing shows many 'sporadic' cases of frontotemporal dementia are actually inherited"
- **Abstract says:** "Among individuals recorded as 'sporadic', 5.5% of ALS and 15.9% of FTD were genetically related to another affected individual in the cohort"
- **Problem:** 15.9% is better rendered as "one in six" than "many", and the finding is relatedness to another affected individual within this cohort — which is evidence of heritable disease masked by reduced penetrance, not a demonstration that each case is inherited. The digest body gets this right; the headline does not.
- **Suggested fix:** "Genetic sleuthing shows one in six 'sporadic' frontotemporal dementia cases is related to another patient"

---

### Study 12: Sleeping light instead of deep is linked to early damage in the brain's small blood vessels
**PMID:** 42779207 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N = 154, mean age 63.26, 41.56% women, WatchPAT-200, PSMD and cortical thickness associations, the REM null and the WMH/PVS nulls are all correctly reported, the language is associational throughout, and the Caveats accurately reflect the authors' own cross-sectional caution. NS fit of 5 is defensible.

---

### Study 13: Four in ten older people with epilepsy struggle with everyday tasks — and one in six at a level seen in dementia
**PMID:** 42704320 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 57, mean age 66.6, FAQ thresholds, 38.6% and 17.5%, financial and memory-dependent clustering, and 4 of 13 worsening over two years are all accurate.

**Issue A. Multivariable predictors apply to the MCI-level outcome only** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Temporal lobe localization, epilepsy onset before age 60 and lower education independently predicted impairment"
- **Abstract says:** "temporal lobe epilepsy (OR = 3.73...), EOE (OR = 6.91...), and lower education (OR = 0.69...) remained independently associated with baseline MCI-level functional impairment. Lower education (OR = 0.62...) was the only factor associated with dementia-level IADL impairment."
- **Problem:** Only education predicted the dementia-level outcome. As written, the sentence sits next to the "17.5% at dementia level" figure and implies all three predictors apply to both.
- **Suggested fix:** "Temporal lobe localization, epilepsy onset before age 60 and lower education independently predicted MCI-level impairment; only lower education predicted dementia-level impairment"

**Issue B. "Decades of it" misdescribes early-onset epilepsy** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the counterintuitive detail that earlier-onset epilepsy — decades of it — predicted worse function in old age"
- **Abstract says:** "early-onset epilepsy (EOE; <60 years)"
- **Problem:** EOE here means onset before age 60 in a cohort with mean age 66.6 — for many participants that is a few years, not decades. The parenthetical invents a duration the study did not measure.
- **Suggested fix:** "the counterintuitive detail that epilepsy beginning before 60 — rather than late-onset epilepsy — predicted worse function in old age"

### Study 17: Most people with advanced dementia do die at home — but who ends up in hospital is not who you'd expect
**PMID:** 40913758 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues (one Moderate)

N = 284, Singapore home-based palliative care service, final place of care defined as the last three days of life, 81.7% home and 9.2% each hospital and inpatient hospice, the better-status/hospital finding, the discomfort/feeding/psychosocial/unemployment predictors of hospice transfer, and the null for stable sociodemographic factors are all accurate.

**Issue A. Headline reports a different outcome from the one the study measured, and overgeneralizes the population** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Most people with advanced dementia do die at home — but who ends up in hospital is not who you'd expect"
- **Abstract says:** "this study's aim was to identify factors affecting the relatively understudied concept of final place of care (where care was received in the last three days of life...)"; "A retrospective cohort study was conducted using secondary data (electronic medical records) from 284 individuals enrolled in a home-based palliative care service for people with advanced dementia in Singapore."
- **Problem:** The 81.7% figure is final place of *care*, not place of *death* — a distinction the paper exists to make and that the digest's own pitch depends on. The headline also generalizes from a cohort already enrolled in a home palliative care service to "people with advanced dementia" in general, who have very different odds of dying at home.
- **Suggested fix:** "Most people with advanced dementia on a home palliative care service spend their final days at home — but who ends up in hospital is not who you'd expect"

### Study 18: People with Down syndrome understand what dementia is — their families often won't discuss it
**PMID:** 42725843 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Study design (qualitative, applied thematic analysis with inductive and deductive coding), Australian setting, and the three core findings are accurately rendered, and the digest correctly notes that no sample size is given in the abstract.

**Issue A. Quantifiers strengthened beyond the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "several were reluctant to raise it with their relative, and most lacked confidence in existing diagnostic pathways" / headline: "their families often won't discuss it"
- **Abstract says:** "Families were aware of the association between Down syndrome and Alzheimer's disease, but some were reluctant to discuss this with their family member. Families lacked confidence in current dementia diagnostic pathways."
- **Problem:** "Some" becomes "several" and then "often" in the headline; "families lacked confidence" (unquantified) becomes "most". In a qualitative study with an unstated N, these numerical intensifiers are not supportable.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "People with Down syndrome understand what dementia is — some families are reluctant to discuss it"; body: "some were reluctant to raise it with their relative, and families lacked confidence in existing diagnostic pathways"

**Issue B. Background genetics presented inside the study paragraph** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Families knew about the strong link between Down syndrome and Alzheimer's — roughly a lifetime certainty of Alzheimer's pathology, given trisomy of the amyloid precursor protein gene"
- **Abstract says:** "People with Down syndrome are at high risk of Alzheimer's disease."
- **Problem:** The APP-trisomy mechanism and the near-universal pathology figure are correct background but are not in this abstract, and the sentence construction implies they are what families reported knowing. Also note the "single health service in Melbourne" caveat is unverifiable from the abstract, which gives no recruitment site.
- **Suggested fix:** "Families knew about the strong link between Down syndrome and Alzheimer's (background: trisomy of the amyloid precursor protein gene means near-universal Alzheimer's pathology by midlife — not from this paper)"
